newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Toyota rewards Australia for brake on tariff cuts.
newsitem.headline: Toyota rewards Australia for brake on tariff cuts.

text.p: Japanese car-maker Toyota Motor Corp on Monday announced an expansion of Australian production in a move hailed by Canberra as vindication of its refusal to slash tariffs on foreign-made cars.
Toyota president Hiroshi Okuda, flanked by Prime Minister John Howard, told a news conference Toyota would begin making a new family car for the Australian market from year 2000.

The new project is part of a plan to spend up to A$1.0 billion (US$740 million) upgrading Toyota's Melbourne plant over the next eight years, almost doubling its annual production to 140,000 cars by 2005, the company said.
The announcement comes two months after Howard rejected the recommendation of an official advisory body for an accelerated drop in tariffs to five percent by 2004 from 22.5 percent now.

Citing concern for an industry employing over 45,000 people, Canberra stuck by the existing timetable for tariff cuts which would see them fall to 15 percent by 2000 and then to 10 percent five years later.
"This announcement is vindication of the decision taken by my government two months ago in relation to long-term policy for the motor manufacturing industry in Australia," Howard said.
Howard also hinted that the other three locally based car-makers -- Ford Motor Co, General Motors Holden and Mitsubishi Motors -- were expected to follow suit.
"We were told both publicly and privately that the decision we were going to take would have an influence in general terms on the long-term investment plans of all of the companies," Howard said.
Mitsubishi has said it is likely to invest A$450 million in a new Australian-made model after Canberra's decision to put the brakes on tariffs, but it has yet to approve the expenditure.
The car-makers want to slow the pace of tariff cuts, arguing that tariff and non-tariff barriers remain higher in their key export markets, especially in Asia.
Australia, as member of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum, says it remains committed to free trade by 2010.
Toyota's Okuda on Monday said Canberra's June decision on tariffs gave the company the green light to expand in Australia.
"I'm pleased to say that this policy direction gives us the confidence to proceed with plans for Australia," he said.
Australia's car market has been stagnant, with no growth in new-vehicle demand for nearly 20 years and patchy profitability.

Toyota's Melbourne production line will this year break even for the first time since it opened in 1994, the company said on Monday. Toyota Australia and Mitsubishi Australia both reported operating losses for calendar 1996.
But Howard said Australian car sales were picking up.
"As far as volume is concerned the indication is that this year will be a lot better...There are real prospects that it could be the second best year on record," he said.
Toyota said its new Australian-made large family model would be a six-cylinder car based on the U.S.-made Avalon. The first models are due to roll off the production line here in 2000.
Toyota is also considering establishing a research and development centre in Australia, the company said.
